title: The Kiss-up Kick-down Pattern
description: A common toxic behavior where a person is charming and submissive to those above them but cruel, dismissive, or bullying to those below them. It’s a strategy for climbing hierarchies by managing up and crushing down.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: A common toxic behavior where a person is charming and submissive to those above them but cruel, dismissive, or bullying to those below them. It’s a strategy for climbing hierarchies by managing up and crushing down.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A middle manager is all smiles and “great idea, boss” in executive meetings but screams at his direct reports afterward.
A senior partner is incredibly polite to clients but treats the support staff like furniture.
An employee takes credit for the team’s work when presenting to leadership but blames the team when things go wrong.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Sudden personality shift when a higher‑up enters or leaves the room.
Excessive flattery toward superiors, often public.
Taking credit downward, deflecting blame upward.
Zero loyalty to anyone who can’t help their career.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: To superiors: “I completely agree, that’s brilliant.”
To subordinates: “You’re lucky to have a job.”
“They don’t need to know the details; just get it done.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You notice you’re treated differently by the same person depending on who’s watching.
The person has no genuine relationships with peers—only with those above and below.
They never defend their team to upper management.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: It’s a pure power strategy. Resources and promotions come from above, so energy is spent there. Below, there are no consequences for cruelty if the higher‑ups never see it. The pattern emerges from low empathy and high ambition.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you’re above them, look past their charm and ask their direct reports about their leadership.
If you’re below them, document everything. Build relationships with other managers to create a safety net.
If you’re a peer, don’t trust them with anything that could be used against you. They will drop you the moment you’re no longer useful.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you can win their favor by being loyal. They see loyalty as a weakness to exploit.
Confronting them publicly without evidence; they are skilled at playing the victim to superiors.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A department head praises his VP constantly. In a meeting, the VP announces a new initiative; the department head nods vigorously. The moment the VP leaves, the department head turns to his team and says, “This is the stupidest idea yet. You’d better make it work or your bonuses are gone.” One team member quits and tells the VP during the exit interview. The VP is shocked; the charm had worked for years.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Watch how someone treats the waiter, the intern, the janitor. The person who is nice to you but nasty to them is not nice.
